journeys.name: Chili Pepper
journeys.tagline: An American fruit that conquered Asia in 200 years
journeys.framing: A set of American fruits that, within about 150 years of 1492, rewired how India, Thailand, China, Korea and Hungary taste heat, replacing or joining older pungencies (black pepper, Sichuan pepper, mustard, ginger) almost everywhere it landed.

stops.note: No arrival: this is the homeland. Wild Capsicum diversified here, and local peoples brought C. baccatum (the aji amarillo lineage) into cultivation in the Andean foothills and adjacent lowlands; C. pubescens was domesticated at mid-elevations nearby. There was no single 'chili domestication': five species were domesticated independently — C. annuum in south-central Mexico, C. baccatum in the Andean foothills, C. chinense in north-central Amazonia, C. pubescens in the mid-elevation Andes, and C. frutescens probably in Central America or the Caribbean.
stops.use: Fresh and later dried pods ground into sauces; heat, colour and vitamin-rich seasoning for bland, filling staples (maize, potatoes, quinoa), plus medicinal uses. Birds, immune to capsaicin, dispersed the wild seeds. Heat became a farmable, storable flavour rather than a foraged one.

highlightDish.name: Llajwa
highlightDish.blurb: Bolivia's raw ground sauce of locoto (rocoto) chili with tomato and herbs, ground on a stone batan.
highlightDish.why: It is the homeland's own format, chili pounded fresh into a table sauce rather than cooked into a stew, and it shows the two American partners, chili and tomato, already paired at source.

stops.note: C. annuum, domesticated in south-central Mexico, arrived overland through Indigenous farming and trade networks centuries before the Aztec (Mexica) state; by the 1400s market vendors in Tenochtitlan sold dozens of named varieties, fresh, dried and smoked. Chili became a system, not a spice: heat levels, colours and smoke were deliberately graded and combined, the template every later cuisine would copy with local ingredients.
stops.use: The core technique was transformation by drying and smoking (the chipotle is a smoked jalapeño) and by grinding toasted dried chilies with tomato, squash seeds and herbs on a metate into sauces: chilmolli, 'chili sauce,' in Nahuatl. Chili was food, medicine (toothache, coughs) and tribute.

highlightDish.name: Chilmolli
highlightDish.blurb: Pre-Hispanic chili sauce, the ancestor of mole: turkey or game in a ground sauce of toasted dried chilies, tomato and seeds.
highlightDish.why: It proves the complex chili sauce is Indigenous, not colonial. Sahagun records no chocolate in savory mollis — the chocolate-rich mole poblano is a later, colonial-era development, not a pre-Hispanic recipe.

stops.note: Columbus's ships from the Caribbean in 1493; Columbus described the local aji in his journal on 1 January 1493 as more valuable than black or melegueta pepper, and Chanca, physician on the second voyage, brought seeds back. Monks grew peppers as garden curiosities and early adopters in Spain and Portugal began eating them. A perishable American fruit became a durable European spice powder — the form in which chili could travel on any ship and keep for years.
stops.use: In Iberia the key move was drying: fresh pods spoiled on long journeys, dried pods kept. In La Vera, pods were smoke-dried over oak and ground into pimenton; elsewhere sweet and hot powders seasoned sausages and stews as a cheap local substitute for imported black pepper.

highlightDish.name: Chorizo seasoned with pimenton de la Vera
highlightDish.blurb: Pork sausage coloured and preserved with smoked ground chili.
highlightDish.why: It shows Spain's specific transformation — smoke plus grinding plus pork fat — and pimenton's antimicrobial, colour-giving role in cured meat, not just heat for its own sake.

stops.note: Carried by the Portuguese, who had it in Brazil and Iberia; food historian Lizzie Collingham notes it was planted in Iberia after 1492 and that by 1528 at the latest the Portuguese had introduced it to the Malabar Coast, with several varieties being grown in Goa. Exact first-landing dates and the Africa-to-Goa hops proposed by some writers are debated. Within generations India made chili so completely its own that its American origin was forgotten.
stops.use: Fresh green and dried red chilies entered pickles, masalas and daily cooking across castes and regions, joining and often displacing black pepper as the everyday source of heat because chili was far cheaper to grow locally. Goan Catholic cooks, free to eat pork, ground dried red chilies into vinegar-based marinades.

highlightDish.name: Pork vindalho
highlightDish.blurb: Pork marinated and cooked in palm vinegar, garlic and dried red chilies, from the Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos (meat in wine and garlic).
highlightDish.why: Two colonial substitutions in one pot (palm vinegar for wine, American chili for part of the heat) make it the clearest edible record of the Goa landing. Fact-check: traditional vindalho contains NO potato; potatoes entered restaurant versions through confusion of Portuguese alhos (garlic) with Hindi aloo (potato).

stops.note: Reached Siam during the Ayutthaya period, in the 16th-17th centuries, most plausibly via Portuguese traders (Portugal took Malacca in 1511 and sent envoys to Ayutthaya the same year) and regional trade. The precise carrier and date are NOT documented; claims of a single neat 'via Malacca in 1600' handoff should be read as approximate.
stops.use: Before chili, Thai heat came from black pepper and other pungent roots. Chili, fresh, dried and pounded, moved into the mortar: curry pastes and nam prik (chili dips/pastes) were rebuilt around it, combined with shrimp paste, garlic, lime and fermented fish. Small, fierce bird's eye chilies (prik ki nu) became the signature form. Heat shifted from peppery warmth to capsaicin fire layered with sour, salty and fermented flavours.

highlightDish.name: Nam prik kapi
highlightDish.blurb: Pounded dip of fresh and dried chilies with shrimp paste, garlic, lime juice and palm sugar, eaten with vegetables and fried fish.
highlightDish.why: The mortar paste is where the substitution actually happened (an older black-pepper paste format refilled with an American ingredient), so the dish documents the technique, not just the flavour.

stops.note: Chili first appears in a Chinese written record in 1591, near the coast (Gao Lian, writing near modern Shanghai, treated it as an ornamental). From the coasts it travelled inland via trade and migration and was taken up first not in Sichuan but in landlocked, salt-poor Guizhou in the early Qing period. In China chili began as a poor person's salt substitute and flavouring of necessity in the southwest, carrying a low-status, 'coarse' reputation among elites for over a century.
stops.use: A local chronicler in 1722 recorded that 'sea pepper' (hai jiao, the name betraying its maritime arrival) was used by Miao communities to replace salt, which the imperial salt monopoly made expensive. Chili was eaten fresh, dried, fermented and scorched; it flavoured sauces, vinegar, oils and preserved vegetables.

highlightDish.name: Scorched chili dip (hujiao / burnt-chili zhan shui)
highlightDish.blurb: Dried chilies blackened, pounded and mixed as a dipping seasoning.
highlightDish.why: It is Guizhou's necessity cooking in miniature — maximum flavour extracted from one cheap dried ingredient where salt itself was unaffordable.

stops.note: Not from Spain directly: peppers reached Hungary through Ottoman mediation and Balkan trade during the Ottoman occupation (1526-1699), first recorded in the 16th century as decorative, supposedly poisonous plants in aristocratic gardens.
stops.use: The Hungarian transformation was to dry and grind peppers into paprika. Herdsmen and peasants adopted it through the 18th century as a cheap substitute for black pepper, a substitution boosted when Napoleonic-era blockades made black pepper scarce; by the 19th century the Szeged and Kalocsa regions were breeding graded sweet-to-hot paprikas and blooming the powder in fat at the start of cooking. (It did NOT fully replace black pepper — the old journey copy was wrong: pepper remained in the kitchen.)

highlightDish.name: Gulyas (goulash soup)
highlightDish.blurb: Beef, onion and abundant paprika bloomed in fat.
highlightDish.why: It corrects the usual shorthand twice over. Goulash existed for centuries before paprika, and paprika did not fully replace black pepper in Hungarian cooking: it displaced pepper in peasant and national dishes while pepper remained. The dish is evidence of a 19th-century reinvention, not an ancient recipe.

stops.note: Chili reached Sichuan late, carried inland from Hunan as Hunanese migrants repopulated Sichuan in the Qing period, centuries after its 1591 coastal debut. Sichuan was not an early adopter; it was the last of China's now-spicy southwestern provinces to take chili up at scale.
stops.use: Sichuan's original contribution was a pairing: American capsaicin heat (la) fused with the indigenous numbing tingle (ma) of Sichuan pepper, plus fermentation — notably Pixian doubanjiang, broad beans fermented with chili. Dried chilies were fried in oil to perfume it, fresh and pickled chilies added sour heat. The mala combination redefined Sichuan identity in the Qing period and after.

highlightDish.name: Mapo tofu
highlightDish.blurb: Tofu in a chili-bean-paste sauce with minced meat and ground Sichuan pepper, created c. 1874 at a Chengdu restaurant run by the Chen family (the name refers to the pockmarked proprietor).
highlightDish.why: It is datable, it contains the full mala equation (fermented chili paste plus Sichuan pepper) in one bowl, and its youth is the point: Sichuan's most famous flavour is younger than the telephone patent era.

stops.note: Chili was introduced to Korea in the early 17th century via Portuguese-linked trade (the first Korean mention is in the encyclopedia Jibong yuseol, 1614; some accounts route it via Japan during the Imjin War period, and the exact path is debated). For two centuries it remained a minor ingredient. Sun-dried and ground into flakes and powder (gochugaru), chili entered ferments — and chili use in kimchi became widespread only in the 19th century. Whole-head napa-cabbage kimchi in its modern form is described only in the late-19th-century cookbook Siuijeonseo.
stops.use: Chili recoloured a national food: kimchi went from white/pale to red, gained preservative and appetite-driving heat, and kimjang, the communal winter kimchi-making, was later inscribed by UNESCO (2013) as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

highlightDish.name: Baechu kimchi (whole napa-cabbage kimchi)
highlightDish.blurb: Salted cabbage fermented with gochugaru, garlic, ginger and jeotgal (salted seafood).
highlightDish.why: It is a 19th-century invention wearing ancient clothes, and it proves the Atlas point perfectly: an American ingredient can become so central that a cuisine's identity is now unthinkable without it.

journeys.name: Tomato
journeys.tagline: Feared as poison in Europe, then adopted by everyone
journeys.framing: A sour Andean berry that Europe feared, Italy rebuilt into a sauce civilisation, and industry then turned into the world's default red flavour, from curry bases to ketchup to Chinese home cooking.

stops.note: No arrival: the wild homeland. Cherry-sized wild tomatoes grew in the wet eastern Andean foothills of southern Ecuador and northern Peru, and, on the genomic account, local peoples cultivated intermediate forms into medium-sized fruit. The evidence here is genetic and botanical, not culinary: no menu, recipe or named dish from this stage survives.
stops.use: Small, intensely flavoured fruit eaten fresh and cultivated at small scale; nothing like the large, mild, watery modern tomato.

highlightDish.name: The wild cherry tomato itself
highlightDish.blurb: Cherry-sized, sour fruit, closer to a condiment berry than a vegetable.
highlightDish.why: No named Andean tomato dish from this stage survives, and inventing one would be dishonest. The fruit itself is the honest highlight: this is what the tomato was before Mexico and Europe changed it.

stops.note: Reached Mesoamerica from South America in pre-Columbian times; the route and mechanism are unknown. The large-fruited tomato was completed in Mexico (the traditional account says domestication happened here; 2020 genomic work points to a two-stage process starting in Ecuador and Peru, so the sequence is debated). By the 1400s Tlatelolco market vendors sold large, small, leaf and 'serpent' tomatoes in colours from yellow to bright red (Florentine Codex).
stops.use: Eaten ripe and cooked with chili, the pairing that would later circle the planet: sauces of tomato with chili and ground squash seeds, ground in the molcajete/metate tradition.

highlightDish.name: Salsa roja (tomatl, chili and squash-seed sauce)
highlightDish.blurb: Tomatoes ground with chilies and seeds, served with meats and tortillas.
highlightDish.why: Documented in the Florentine Codex market lists. It establishes that the tomato's defining role, cooked sour sauce base, is Mexican before it is Italian.

stops.note: Spanish ships carried seed from Mexico to Seville in the early 16th century; Spain and Italy were the first Europeans to adopt the tomato as food. The first known European description is Italian: herbalist Pietro Andrea Mattioli in 1544, calling it 'golden apple' (pomo d'oro) and classifying it as a nightshade and mandrake relative, yet recording that some ate it as eggplant was eaten.
stops.use: Mattioli recorded the earliest European preparation: eaten like eggplant, fried in oil with salt and pepper. Europe split in two: the Spanish-Italian south began eating the tomato in the 1500s while France and northern Europe grew it as an ornamental and regarded it with suspicion as a nightshade relative.

highlightDish.name: Fried golden apple, Mattioli-style
highlightDish.blurb: Sliced tomato fried in oil with salt and black pepper, eaten like eggplant.
highlightDish.why: The earliest European tomato preparation actually described, and its plainness is the evidence: in 1544 the tomato entered Europe as a fried curiosity, not a sauce.

stops.note: Established in Spanish-ruled Naples through the 1600s. Antonio Latini, steward to the Spanish viceroy's household, published the earliest surviving European tomato sauce recipes in Lo scalco alla moderna (1692/1694): a sauce alla spagnola for boiled meats, NOT a pasta sauce. The first known printed pairing of tomato sauce with pasta came almost a century later, in Francesco Leonardi's L'Apicio moderno (1790).
stops.use: Latini's sauce (roasted tomatoes chopped with onion, chili, salt, oil and vinegar) was a condiment for boiled meats. Through the 1800s poor Neapolitans put tomato on flatbread and pasta at scale (54 pizzerias recorded in Naples by 1807), then canning made it southern Italy's cheap, storable acidity and colour.

highlightDish.name: Spaghetti al pomodoro, after Leonardi (1790)
highlightDish.blurb: Pasta with cooked tomato sauce.
highlightDish.why: The first documented pasta-tomato pairing in print. It corrects the old claim that Naples had pasta and pizza sauce by c. 1700: that was roughly a century too early.

stops.note: Two waves, often conflated. The tomato first reached India with the Portuguese in the 16th century, alongside chili. Widespread cultivation and kitchen adoption, however, came under the British in the 19th century: commercial cultivation is recorded around Dehradun from c. 1815-1830, spreading to hill stations and then nationally through the 20th century.
stops.use: Cooked down fresh or as puree into the base gravy: bulk, mild sourness and umami, partly displacing older souring agents (tamarind, kokum, curd, dried mango) depending on region. In the south it joined tamarind in rasam and sambar-style cooking rather than erasing them. India is now the world's second-largest tomato producer.

highlightDish.name: Tomato rasam
highlightDish.blurb: Thin, peppery South Indian soup of tomato with tamarind, black pepper and cumin, eaten with rice.
highlightDish.why: Rasam shows the negotiation, not the takeover: an older tamarind-and-pepper sour soup absorbs the newcomer as co-souring agent, which is exactly how the tomato entered most Indian kitchens, as a base, not a star.

stops.note: A return journey: North America received the tomato from Europe, not directly from Mexico. Jefferson grew tomatoes at Monticello in 1781; the fruit was eaten in Louisiana by 1812 but reached the northeastern states only around 1835. In 1876 Henry J. Heinz launched his bottled tomato ketchup in Pittsburgh, standardising rather than inventing it: the first published tomato ketchup recipe was James Mease's in 1812.
stops.use: Industrial: cooked, sweetened, vinegared and bottled. The word ketchup descends from Chinese ke-tsiap, a pickled-fish sauce, via 18th-century British mushroom and walnut ketchups. Heinz's version was eventually preservative-free and high-vinegar, in clear glass to advertise purity.

highlightDish.name: Heinz Tomato Ketchup itself
highlightDish.blurb: The branded industrial sauce, served with everything.
highlightDish.why: At this stop the 'dish' really is the transformation, fresh fruit to shelf-stable global condiment. Any copy saying 'Heinz invented tomato ketchup in 1876' is wrong by 64 years.

stops.note: No new arrival; a delayed acceptance. France, which had grown the tomato as an ornamental and suspicion object in the 1500s-1700s (the pomme d'amour), adopted it through Provencal and Mediterranean cooking in the 19th century, then canonised it: Auguste Escoffier codified sauce tomate as one of the five mother sauces in Le Guide Culinaire (1903).
stops.use: Tomato with pork belly, onion, herbs, garlic and roux: a foundation sauce from which other sauces are derived, the form in which French technique exported tomato cookery globally.

highlightDish.name: Sauce tomate (Escoffier's mother sauce)
highlightDish.blurb: Tomato with pork belly, onion, herbs, garlic and roux.
highlightDish.why: Documentary proof of canonisation, dated and printed. It contrasts with the Naples stop: Naples made the tomato popular from below, Paris certified it from above.

stops.note: The tomato (fan qie, 'foreign eggplant') reached China in the Ming period via maritime trade and was long grown as an ornamental: into the 1880s local evaluations still called it pretty but inedible. Eating it spread through Western restaurants in late-Qing and early-Republican treaty ports, above all cosmopolitan Shanghai, whose surrounding farmers began growing tomatoes to supply them.
stops.use: Chinese cooks adopted the tomato on Chinese terms: quick, hot, brief cooking. In the 1920s-30s Shanghai restaurants sold stir-fried tomato with scrambled egg, a technique with a two-millennia Chinese pedigree applied to the foreign fruit; home-cooked records appear in the 1940s, after which it became a nationwide household standard. China is now the world's largest tomato producer.

highlightDish.name: Stir-fried tomato and scrambled eggs
highlightDish.blurb: Soft scrambled egg folded with juicy, lightly sweetened tomato.
highlightDish.why: The adoption mechanism made edible: an ancient Chinese technique domesticating a Ming-dynasty ornamental. It corrects the old copy, which said Guangzhou c. 1920 (it was Shanghai restaurants in the 1920s-30s, home cooking in the 1940s).

journeys.name: Potato
journeys.tagline: The Andean tuber that fed industrial Europe
journeys.framing: The Andes' freeze-dried survival ration that crossed the Atlantic as a sailor's curiosity, spent two centuries feared as poisonous animal feed, then became the crop that fed Europe's industrial working class, emptied Ireland, and ended up identical in every fast-food fryer on Earth.

stops.note: No arrival: the homeland. Communities around the lake selected wild bitter potatoes; the FAO dates domestication to about 8,000 years ago (academic range 6,000-10,000). The archaeological record shows chuno production at Tiwanaku on the Collao Plateau before the Inca Empire, and Jose de Acosta described chuno in 1590.
stops.use: Freeze-drying, not cooking, was the transformative technique: bitter frost-resistant potatoes spread on the Altiplano to freeze overnight and sun-thaw by day, trampled over days until storable for years. Fresh potatoes went into stews; dried ones were ground into flour to thicken soups or rehydrated. The Inca stored chuno in state warehouses and marched it with armies.

highlightDish.name: Chupe de papas
highlightDish.blurb: Potatoes and rehydrated chuno simmered into a thick highland soup.
highlightDish.why: The dish that only exists because of the processing innovation: the chew and body of the stew come from a tuber that was dried years earlier and carried hundreds of miles, which is the whole Andean point.

stops.note: Spanish ships returning from the Andes, presumed to have carried tubers as ships' provisions. The Canaries are the first place outside the Americas with documented potato cultivation: a 28 November 1567 receipt records potatoes shipped from Las Palmas to Antwerp, and Seville hospital records show them on sale by 1573. Genetic work on surviving Canarian landraces supports multiple early introductions rather than a single landing.
stops.use: Sailors ate them on voyages; in Spain they were hospital and poorhouse food and a botanist's curiosity (Carolus Clusius illustrated 'Papas Peruanorum' in 1601). The Canaries became the tuber's first European seed bank.

highlightDish.name: Papas arrugadas con mojo
highlightDish.blurb: Small potatoes boiled unpeeled in heavily salted water until a wrinkled salt crust forms, served with mojo picon (garlic, chili, cumin, vinegar).
highlightDish.why: Cooked from papas antiguas, Andean-descended landraces with Protected Designation of Origin status that Smithsonian reporting calls direct descendants of the 16th-century arrivals: a living fossil of the first European potato.

stops.note: Arrived between 1586 and 1600, most plausibly via Spain; the exact carrier is not documented, and the famous stories crediting Raleigh or Drake are myths with no evidence. By the 1700s the potato was the subsistence crop of the rural poor; by the early 1800s Ireland depended almost entirely on one high-yielding clone, the Irish Lumper, a monoculture with no genetic backup.
stops.use: Boiled in their skins and eaten with buttermilk or salt, the potato became a near-total diet: the poorest labourers ate 8 to 14 pounds a day. More than a third of the harvest also fed the cattle that were Ireland's main export.

highlightDish.name: Boxty
highlightDish.blurb: Grated raw potato mixed with mashed potato, formed into pancakes and fried.
highlightDish.why: Poverty cooking in its purest form, the tuber stretched with itself and fried in whatever fat existed: exactly what the potato was in Ireland before 1845.

stops.note: Sixteen Scotch-Irish families settled Nutfield (soon renamed Londonderry, now Derry) in April 1719 and planted the first permanent potato field crop in New England. Correction: not the first potato planting in North America, the English had grown potatoes in Bermuda and Virginia in the early 1600s, but the first permanent field crop in what became the United States, and the one that stuck.
stops.use: A field crop for settler farms, grown alongside flax; the potato entered American English as the 'Irish potato.' English neighbours were suspicious: a Scotch-Irish family tradition holds that neighbours given seed tubers threw them in a swamp fearing poison.

highlightDish.name: New potatoes boiled in their skins, with salt
highlightDish.blurb: The settler's staple: no sauce, no technique beyond a pot of water.
highlightDish.why: The absence of a recipe is the evidence. The potato entered America as survival food, not cuisine; the first American recipe of note came eighty years later, when Jefferson served 'potatoes fried in the French manner' at a White House dinner in 1802.

stops.note: Not the tuber: potatoes had been grown in Bavaria since 1647 and in Brandenburg gardens since the 1650s. What arrived in 1756 was paperwork, Frederick II's 24 March Kartoffelbefehl ordering Silesian officials to plant potatoes (one of about fifteen such decrees, with pastors enlisted to preach the tuber). The people largely ignored them; widespread adoption came only after the Napoleonic wars ended in 1815. The famous story of Frederick posting guards so peasants would steal the tubers is a myth: he himself never ate a potato.
stops.use: The decrees promoted field-scale planting as famine insurance after the Pomeranian famine. The real engine of adoption was hunger, not royal marketing: successive famines did what fifteen decrees could not, and the potato became the German peasant staple of the 19th century.

highlightDish.name: Pellkartoffeln mit Quark
highlightDish.blurb: Potatoes boiled 'in jackets', peeled at the table and eaten with quark, chives and salt.
highlightDish.why: The dish the decrees were really about: the cheapest complete peasant meal in northern Germany, adopted through necessity rather than trickery.

stops.note: Antoine-Augustin Parmentier's campaign. An army pharmacist taken prisoner in Prussia during the Seven Years' War and fed on potatoes, he won the 1771 Besancon Academy prize, hosted all-potato dinners for guests including Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier, and saw his Treatise on the Culture and Use of the Potato printed by royal order in 1789. (The guarded demonstration field at Sablons was attributed to him posthumously and is near-certainly apocryphal; the bad harvests of 1785 did more for adoption than any stunt.)
stops.use: Propaganda as much as science: elite endorsement plus public demonstration. The potato went from a crop the Paris Parlement had restricted in 1748 amid claims it caused leprosy, to a patriotic republican staple. France's population grew roughly 50 percent between 1770 and 1820, and the potato gets part of the credit.

highlightDish.name: Hachis Parmentier
highlightDish.blurb: Chopped leftover beef (traditionally pot-au-feu meat) under a layer of mashed potato, baked golden.
highlightDish.why: Starting in the 1870s, France began naming potato dishes after Parmentier. The dish is later than the man, which is the point: the feared tuber became a namesake honour, absorbed so completely into French cooking that it carries his name.

stops.note: Two landings. The Portuguese brought the potato to India's west coast in the 17th century: Edward Terry recorded potatoes at a banquet at Ajmer in 1675. The British then pushed it in Bengal in the late 1700s as a famine-proof crop, reportedly offering 100 rupees to farmers who would switch, and by the end of the 18th century it was cultivated across the northern hill areas.
stops.use: From a colonial garden novelty to a core Indian vegetable: dry-fried with spices, stuffed into breads and pastries, simmered in curries. It asked nothing of the cook that Indian kitchens did not already have, turmeric, cumin, mustard oil, a tawa, and it bulked out meals where meat was absent for religious or economic reasons. India is now the world's second-largest potato producer.

highlightDish.name: Aloo gobi
highlightDish.blurb: Potatoes and cauliflower dry-fried with turmeric, cumin and ginger, eaten with roti.
highlightDish.why: It shows the potato not as a colonial import or a side dish but as an Indian vegetable among vegetables, cooked with the standard home tempering: total domestication into the everyday sabzi.

stops.note: The modern fry was born in Paris around 1855, according to food historian Pierre Leclercq: not the first fried potato, but the crisp, twice-fried street-food form. Two myths die here: the Belgian claim that Meuse villagers were frying potatoes in the 1680s (an unproduced manuscript, a 1980s misreading), and the story that WWI doughboys coined 'French fries' (a 1990s invention). What survives is the technique: the double fry, and the fry shack as an institution.
stops.use: Street vendors fried potato strips in bubbling fat and sold them in paper cones: the first potato form that was a standalone business rather than something cooked at home. The Belgians made it national culture through the fritkot (fry shack), served with mayonnaise and dozens of sauces.

highlightDish.name: Frites
highlightDish.blurb: Potato strips fried twice, crisp outside and fluffy inside, served in a paper cornet with mayonnaise.
highlightDish.why: It is the technique, not the tuber, that travelled. The fry turned the potato from a boiled staple into a craveable street food, and the fritkot turned a cooking method into a national identity.

stops.note: Catherine the Great promoted cultivation from 1765; in the 1830s-40s the state forced potato planting on peasants. The result was the potato riots: more than 500,000 peasants rising, destroying sowings, being shot, exiled to Siberia or drafted. Within a generation, Lucien Olivier at Moscow's celebrated Hermitage restaurant invented the original Olivier salad in the 1860s: hazel grouse, crayfish tails, potatoes, and a secret mayonnaise-based dressing.
stops.use: From forced crop to haute cuisine: the Soviet simplification, potatoes, carrots, peas, pickles, eggs and mayonnaise, became salat Olivye, the mandatory New Year's dish across the former USSR.

highlightDish.name: Olivier salad (salat Olivye)
highlightDish.blurb: Diced boiled potatoes, carrots, peas, pickles and egg or meat bound with mayonnaise.
highlightDish.why: The riots' endpoint in a bowl. A tuber peasants died refusing became, within decades, the centrepiece of Russia's most festive table, and the Soviet simplification proves the absorption was total.

stops.note: J.R. Simplot's company began commercializing frozen french fries at scale in 1953, after chemist Ray L. Dunlap worked out the blanch-and-quick-freeze process. In 1966/67 (sources differ on the year) Simplot shook hands with McDonald's CEO Ray Kroc on a deal to supply the chain with frozen fries, replacing the fresh-cut potatoes Kroc had insisted on.
stops.use: The frozen fry standardized the potato: Russet Burbank, bred for high solids and good freezing behaviour, blanched, frozen, shipped, and fried to an identical result in every restaurant. The United States became the world's frozen-fry exporter.

highlightDish.name: The frozen French fry
highlightDish.blurb: The industrial product itself.
highlightDish.why: Every earlier stop transformed the potato by cooking or processing it by hand; this stop transformed it by removing the cook. The fry you eat in one city is engineered to be the fry you eat in every city, the final transformation of the journey: from Andean freeze-drying to American deep-freezing.

journeys.name: Coffee
journeys.tagline: From Ethiopian hillsides to every office on Earth
journeys.framing: A wild Ethiopian forest berry that Yemenis learned to roast and brew, Ottomans turned into a public institution, Europeans stole as living plants to grow with enslaved labour across the tropics, and Italians and Swiss industrialists then compressed into shots, froth and powder, making it the world's most ritualised everyday stimulant.

stops.note: No arrival: the homeland. Wild Coffea arabica still grows in the shaded understory of the southwestern Ethiopian cloud forests, and the Kafa people foraged the cherries for centuries. The goat-herder Kaldi story is a legend (written form 1671 at the earliest), but the foraging tradition it points at is real. There is no documented date for first human use in Ethiopia.
stops.use: Cherries were chewed raw or mixed with fat and grain as travel food; later, the long ritual of roasting green beans in a pan, pounding them, and boiling them in the black clay jebena developed. Coffee was domestic and social, not a commodity, and Ethiopia still drinks roughly half of what it grows.

highlightDish.name: Buna (Ethiopian coffee ceremony)
highlightDish.blurb: Green beans roasted in front of guests, ground, boiled in a jebena, poured from a height into small handleless cups in three rounds, abol, tona, baraka ('blessing'), with incense and popcorn.
highlightDish.why: It preserves the oldest layer of coffee use, social and ceremonial, roasted fresh per cup, and shows what coffee was before anyone shipped it: a host's duty, not a product.

stops.note: Cherries and seeds crossed the Red Sea from Ethiopia (traditionally by Sufi dervishes and traders; the exact first crossing is not documented). By the 15th century Yemeni Sufis were cultivating coffee on terraced mountain slopes. The port of Mocha shipped beans across the Islamic world and held the global supply for roughly two centuries; only roasted or boiled beans left Yemen, so they could not be planted abroad.
stops.use: The Yemeni invention was the technology of coffee: roast the beans to develop flavour, grind them, boil the grounds. The drink, qahwa (a word that once meant wine), was taken in Sufi monasteries to stay awake for midnight prayers and study, then moved into daily life.

highlightDish.name: Qishr
highlightDish.blurb: A warm drink brewed from the dried husks of the coffee cherry, spiced with ginger and sometimes cinnamon or cardamom, low in caffeine.
highlightDish.why: It proves Yemeni coffee culture used the whole cherry, not just the seed, and it is the older layer of use surviving inside the monopoly: a drink that needs no roasting at all.

stops.note: Carried up the Red Sea trade into the Arab provinces and to the capital in the early 1500s, by merchants, hajj pilgrims and Sufi dervishes. The Ottoman chronicler Pecevi records that before 1554 there was 'no coffee and no coffeehouses in Rum', and that in that year two merchants, Hakam of Aleppo and Shams of Damascus, opened the first institutional coffeehouses in Tahtakale. (The claim of a 1475 Kiva Han is disputed.)
stops.use: The Ottoman transformation was the coffeehouse and the cezve: coffee ground powder-fine, boiled with water and sugar in a small long-handled pot, served unfiltered so the grounds settle in the cup. Coffeehouses became the city's public living rooms, places of news, poetry, chess and politics. Religious and imperial bans failed; coffeehouses multiplied.

highlightDish.name: Turk kahvesi (Turkish coffee)
highlightDish.blurb: Powder-fine coffee boiled in a cezve, served in a small cup, grounds and all.
highlightDish.why: The Ottoman brewing technology in miniature, the unfiltered cup Europe first encountered, and the fortune-telling in the dregs shows how deep the embedding went: coffee as social ritual, divination and habit at once.

stops.note: Venetian trade had brought coffee drinking to Italy in the early 1600s; England learned it from Ottoman Turkey via the Levant Company. In 1652 Pasqua Rosee, a Greek servant of the Levant merchant Daniel Edwards, opened London's first coffeehouse, a stall against the churchyard wall in St Michael's Alley off Cornhill.
stops.use: Coffee was sold by the 'dish' and drunk Turkish-style, black and gritty. The houses became 'penny universities': for a penny, news, pamphlets, debate, business. Lloyd's of London began as a coffeehouse. Charles II issued a proclamation to suppress the coffeehouses on 29 December 1675, then withdrew it within days under public outcry. (The Pope Clement VIII 'baptising' coffee story is a legend, with no documented decree.)

highlightDish.name: A dish of coffee, Cornhill style (1652)
highlightDish.blurb: Black, gritty, Turkish-brewed, sold with the handbill The Vertue of the 'COFFEE' Drink.
highlightDish.why: The handbill prescribed coffee for dropsy, scurvy, gout and 'mis-carryings', which shows the real evidence of the stop: coffee entered England as a medicine and a novelty, and people acquired the taste before they had any idea what it was for.

stops.note: At the urging of Amsterdam burgomaster Nicolaes Witsen, the Dutch East India Company got live plants out of Yemen's Mocha monopoly in the 1690s (early shipments failed; viable plants reached Java in the late 1690s). By 1719 'Java coffee' was supplying Europe's demand. A Dutch plant gifted to the French at the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) became the ancestor of France's Caribbean coffee. (Baba Budan smuggling seven beans to India is popular legend.)
stops.use: The Dutch transformation was agronomic and commercial: coffee as a plantation monoculture run by colonial labour, processed at scale, shipped in bulk. 'Mocha-Java' became Europe's first named coffee blend.

highlightDish.name: Kopi tubruk
highlightDish.blurb: Javanese coffee: coarse grounds boiled with sugar in the pot and drunk unfiltered, grounds settling at the bottom.
highlightDish.why: The colonial export crop came home as a local brew, unfiltered like the Ottoman original but coarse and sweet, proof that the plantation island developed its own coffee culture under the export machine.

stops.note: The French planted coffee in Saint-Domingue from 1715 (Martinique from the 1720s), from Dutch-Javanese stock via the Paris botanical garden. De Clieu's 1723 voyage to Martinique is his own 1774 account, but Saint-Domingue and Dutch Suriname (1718) already had coffee before him. By 1788 Saint-Domingue exported about 77 million pounds of coffee, roughly half the world's supply, worked by enslaved Africans. The Haitian Revolution (1791-1804) burned it down; by 1801 most plantations were destroyed.
stops.use: Plantation monoculture on an industrial scale, worked by enslaved Africans under brutal conditions. By 1788 French colonial coffee outsold both Mocha and Java beans. The collapse soared prices and pulled Brazil and Cuba into the lead: coffee's geography has been moving ever since.

highlightDish.name: Haitian cafe
highlightDish.blurb: Coffee roasted dark, brewed strong, drunk sweet.
highlightDish.why: It is what remains. Haiti still grows coffee on smallholder plots, and the drink is the everyday residue of the plantation century: the colony that fed the world's habit now drinks the habit itself.

stops.note: In 1727 the Portuguese-Brazilian officer Francisco de Melo Palheta, sent to Cayenne in French Guiana on a border mission, smuggled coffee out. The famous story, that the French governor's wife hid seedlings in a farewell bouquet, is popular legend; what is documented is Palheta's 1733 letter reporting over a thousand seeds and four seedlings. After the Haitian collapse and with American demand rising came a 19th-century explosion: coffee barons, railroads, vast fazendas worked first by enslaved Africans and, after abolition in 1888, by subsidised European immigrants. When the 1929 crash collapsed prices, Getulio Vargas's government bought surpluses and burned them: about 78 million sacks destroyed between 1931 and 1944.
stops.use: For decades a domestic crop, then a state-managed commodity on a continental scale; Brazil's industrialisation was financed by bean money. The crop-burning is the starkest image in coffee history: food destroyed to save a price.

highlightDish.name: Cafezinho
highlightDish.blurb: A tiny cup of strong, dark, heavily sweetened filtered coffee, served to guests everywhere in Brazil, at shops, offices and homes.
highlightDish.why: The world's greatest producer drinks coffee as a miniature ritual of hospitality, not a morning drug; it shows the producer's culture, small, sweet and constant, against the exporter's bulk.

stops.note: No new plant: this stop is about the machine. Angelo Moriondo of Turin patented a steam-driven 'instantaneous' coffee machine in 1884; Luigi Bezzera improved it (1901 patent, adding the portafilter and multiple brew heads) and Desiderio Pavoni commercialised it, debuting the 'Ideale' at the 1906 Milan Fair, promising 1,000 coffees an hour. Achille Gaggia's 1948 lever machine raised pressure to 8-10 atmospheres and created the crema-topped shot we know today.
stops.use: The Italian transformation was extraction under pressure: hot water forced through finely ground coffee in seconds instead of minutes, served in a small cup, drunk standing at the bar. The milk drinks followed: the Viennese Kapuziner, coffee with a little cream named for the brown of Capuchin friars' robes on late-1700s Habsburg menus, became the Italian cappuccino. (The story that the Capuchin friar Marco d'Aviano invented it at Vienna in 1683 is likely apocryphal.)

highlightDish.name: Cappuccino
highlightDish.blurb: Espresso with steamed milk and foam, roughly a third each, drunk in Italy only before late morning.
highlightDish.why: The name carries the whole route in it, from Viennese menus to the Capuchin robe, and the drink is Europe's answer to Ottoman bitterness: keep the strength, soften it with milk, serve it in minutes.

stops.note: No plant at all: this stop is about dehydration. In 1930 the Brazilian government, drowning in surplus (the same surplus it would later burn), asked Nestle to find a use for it; Nestle chemist Max Morgenthaler spent eight years on the problem, and in 1938 the company launched Nescafe, instant coffee, in Switzerland.
stops.use: The 20th-century industrial transformation: coffee as a shelf-stable powder. Earlier steps included vacuum packing (c. 1900), decaffeination, and George Washington's commercial instant coffee in the US from 1909. Instant coffee boomed as military ration coffee in both World Wars, teaching whole populations to drink it. It is still roughly a quarter of world coffee sales.

highlightDish.name: A cup of Nescafe (1938 formula)
highlightDish.blurb: Brewed coffee, spray-dried to powder, reconstituted with hot water.
highlightDish.why: The least romantic coffee in the dossier and therefore the most honest evidence of the stop: coffee as pure logistics, invented to absorb a glut, carried into war by soldiers' ration kits, and still the daily drink of hundreds of millions.

journeys.name: Sugar
journeys.tagline: From a chewed New Guinea stalk to the crop that built the plantation system
journeys.framing: The ingredient that built the plantation system: chewed raw in New Guinea for millennia, crystallized in Gupta India, industrialized by Persian and Arab refiners, and then turned by European empires into the machine that made sweetness cheap and enslaved labour profitable.

sources.label: UNESCO Kuk Swamp archaeology (Wikipedia)
Wikipedia, History of sugar
1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Sugar"
Slavery and Remembrance, Barbados sugar revolution
Wikipedia, Saint-Domingue
Wikipedia, Beet sugar factory
Wikipedia, Sugar industry in Cuba

stops.note: No arrival: the homeland. Archaeology at UNESCO-listed Kuk Swamp puts banana and sugarcane under cultivation 6,900–6,400 years ago in the New Guinea highlands, one of the world's independent inventions of agriculture.
stops.use: Cane was cut fresh and chewed for its juice. It could not be stored, transported far or preserved, so it was food and quick energy on the spot — not a commodity. For five thousand years this was the entire technology of sugar.

highlightDish.name: Fresh-cut sugarcane, chewed raw
highlightDish.blurb: Not a recipe — the point. The sweet stalk, eaten where it grew.
highlightDish.why: For millennia this was all there was. Every later invention (crystals, syrups, refineries) exists to escape the fact that the juice dies with the stalk.

stops.note: Cane reached India through Island Southeast Asia millennia earlier; by the Gupta period it was a familiar field crop. The breakthrough here was a technique, not a plant: boiling juice into crystals.
stops.use: Refiners boiled cane juice into storable granulated crystals — khanda — so sweetness survived harvest season and could travel. Sanskrit śarkarā gave Persian shakar, Arabic sukkar and “sugar”; khanda travelled on into “candy”. Buddhist monks carried the technique to China.

highlightDish.name: Kheer sweetened with khand
highlightDish.blurb: Ancient rice pudding, once honey-sweetened, now sweetened with granulated crystals.
highlightDish.why: It shows what storable sweetness made possible at home: honey's strong flavour was no longer the only way to sweeten milk.

stops.note: Cane came west from India centuries earlier; at the Sasanian-to-Arab-conquest moment, Khuzestan's irrigated plains refined it at scale — the 1911 Britannica records sugar “prepared with art” at Jundi Shapur about the time of the Arab conquest.
stops.use: Water-powered milling and boiling houses turned cane into white and rock sugar at industrial scale; physicians' pharmacopoeia made it a medicine and confectioners grew crystals on sticks. This became the template the Arabs would export across the Mediterranean.

highlightDish.name: Nabat, Persian rock candy
highlightDish.blurb: Glassy crystals grown on wooden sticks, served with tea in Iran to this day.
highlightDish.why: The refinery product in its most literal form: nothing done to the crystal except letting it grow, unchanged since.

stops.note: Arab conquerors brought cane, irrigation and refining to Sicily (827–965); Palermo became their capital, and its cane fields and mills made sugar an Arab-Mediterranean industry. In Europe it stayed medicine, spice and display, rationed by price.
stops.use: A large-scale cane industry for the first time outside Asia: fields, water mills, refineries, and the region's almond-and-rosewater confectionery, now built on crystallized sugar — while Europe, unable to grow cane north of the Mediterranean, became dependent on it.

highlightDish.name: Frutta di Martorana
highlightDish.blurb: Marzipan fruits — almond paste molded and painted — from the Palermo convent legend (founded 1194).
highlightDish.why: A Norman-era convent sweet built from the two Arab imports, sugar and almonds, that define Sicilian pastry; the legend itself is the evidence.

stops.note: Cane came from Sicily at Prince Henry the Navigator's order after wheat faltered; by 1455 Cadamosto reported over 6,000 arrobas, and Madeiran sugar shipped to Flanders by 1472.
stops.use: The plantation formula prototyped: cane fields, water-driven mills fed by levadas, and a growing reliance on enslaved African workers — about 10% of the island's population by the 16th century. The model the Portuguese repeated in the Canaries, São Tomé and Brazil.

highlightDish.name: Bolo de mel
highlightDish.blurb: Dark spiced “honey cake” made with cane molasses — Madeira's oldest dessert, made by the nuns of Santa Clara in Funchal.
highlightDish.why: The island's byproduct made sacred: the molasses waste stream of the sugar industry, baked into a cake that keeps for months — the plantation economy you can eat.

stops.note: English planters shifted from tobacco to sugar in the early 1640s with Dutch capital and Brazilian know-how; within a decade small farms consolidated into large estates worked by enslaved Africans — the “sugar revolution”.
stops.use: Sugar made here was a slave crop from the start. Crushing mills ran around the clock in harvest; muscovado shipped to Amsterdam and London for refining; by 1786 enslaved people were about 79% of the population. Barbados became the Caribbean's entry point for the slavery-and-sugar complex.

highlightDish.name: Rum (Rumbullion)
highlightDish.blurb: Distilled spirit first made in the mid-17th-century Caribbean by enslaved people on sugar plantations, fermenting molasses (1651 Barbados record: “Rumbullion, alias Kill-Divil”).
highlightDish.why: The plantation's waste economy made drinkable: the molasses Europe wouldn't pay to ship became the colonies' own drink, later the currency alcohol of the triangular trade. (Origin credit is traditional; Brazil and India have earlier cane-spirit evidence.)

stops.note: French planters took the Barbados formula to Hispaniola's western third; after the Seven Years' War it expanded explosively, and by the 1780s the colony supplied about 40% of the sugar consumed in Europe — grown by nearly half a million enslaved people.
stops.use: The peak of the system: some 8,000 plantations, workdays up to eighteen hours, over 30,000 new captives landed per year. Sugar reached industrial scale on enslaved labour — until the Haitian Revolution (1791–1804), the only successful slave revolt in history, destroyed it.

highlightDish.name: Rapadou
highlightDish.blurb: Dense cakes of unrefined sugar sold in Haitian markets, eaten and traded today.
highlightDish.why: The plantation's product in its local, unrefined form — what sugar looked like before European refineries got their hands on it.

stops.note: No cane ever grew here — that is the point. Marggraf proved beet roots hold cane-identical sugar in 1747; Achard opened the first beet-sugar factory at Kunern in 1801; Napoleon's 1811 push scaled it. By 1880 beet supplied over half the world's sugar.
stops.use: Refined white sugar stopped being a colonial luxury and became a temperate-world commodity grown with free labour; Central European pastry culture — layer cakes, glazes, jams — was built on it. The plantation system's last structural advantage, that only colonies could make sugar, collapsed.

highlightDish.name: Sachertorte
highlightDish.blurb: The chocolate-apricot layer cake Franz Sacher created in 1832 for Prince Metternich.
highlightDish.why: Its glaze and crumb demand refined white sugar in quantity — the flagship of a pastry culture that could only exist once beet made sweetness a temperate commodity.

stops.note: Cuba's cane rose after the Haitian Revolution collapsed Saint-Domingue; US investment industrialized it, and output grew from about 1M tons (1895) to over 5M (1925). Cuba remained the world's largest sugar producer until the 1960s.
stops.use: A monoculture economy on an industrial scale: mills, railways and seasonal wage labour replacing the old slave gangs after abolition — proof that abolition ended slavery without ending the sugar machine.

highlightDish.name: Mojito
highlightDish.blurb: White rum, lime, mint and muddled cane sugar.
highlightDish.why: By 1920 Havana cane sugar was so cheap it could be spent freely in a working-class drink — sweetness as nothing special, the commodity at its most casual.

journeys.name: Tea
journeys.tagline: One leaf, a hundred reinventions: medicine, ritual, currency, commodity
journeys.framing: One evergreen species, Camellia sinensis, that moved from a southwest-China medicinal brew into a codified Tang ritual, a Song competitive art, a Tibetan necessity, a Japanese religion, a European luxury, a British commodity worth wars, and finally a colonial plantation industry, with every stop changing the form of the drink.

sources.label: Wikipedia, History of tea
Meegahakumbura et al. 2017, tea domestication genetics (Frontiers in Plant Science)
Wikipedia, Tea Horse Road
Wikipedia, Robert Fortune
Jane Pettigrew, the history of Ceylon tea (teamuse.com)

stops.note: The homeland: wild Camellia sinensis grows as tall trees in these mountains; villages chewed, pickled and fermented the leaves as food long before it was a drink. Genetics finds three independent domestication lineages — the China lineage and an Indian Assam lineage are separate.
stops.use: Leaves eaten raw, chewed as a stimulant and fermented into food — the plant was medicine and stimulant food, not a beverage ritual. The 1500 BCE date is a popular-history estimate, not archaeology; the Shen Nong 2737 BCE story is legend.

highlightDish.name: Sheng (raw) pu'er tea
highlightDish.blurb: Large-leaf Yunnan tea, sun-dried and pressed, aged like the brick teas of later trade.
highlightDish.why: The homeland's own format — minimally transformed large-leaf tea from living ancient trees, before courts, connoisseurs and empires touched it.

stops.note: Tea travelled east with Qin-Han unification; the oldest physical evidence is the Han Yangling Mausoleum of Emperor Jing (d. 141 BCE), where a brick of fine-bud tea was buried with the emperor — residue that does not grow near Xi'an, so it was deliberately imported.
stops.use: Fine-bud tea as imperial grave goods and elite tribute; Han sources treat it mainly as medicine and status drink. The earliest written reference is the 59 BCE Tong Yue slave contract.

highlightDish.name: Imperial fine-bud tea
highlightDish.blurb: The burial tea — young unopened buds laid with an emperor.
highlightDish.why: Nobody buries a peasant's brew with an emperor; the grave good is the evidence that tea had become a prestige object by the Western Han.

stops.note: Lu Yu (733–804) wrote the Cha Jing around 760, describing the plant, processing and brewing in ten chapters — native demand, not trade, formalising the drink.
stops.use: Tang tea was steamed, crushed and compressed into cakes; to drink, a cake was roasted, ground and boiled with a pinch of salt, with graded water and timed boils — brewing as a connoisseur's discipline, later the imperial tribute system that made some cakes dearer than gold.

highlightDish.name: Tang boiled cake tea with salt
highlightDish.blurb: Ground cake boiled to a froth, light and unsweetened.
highlightDish.why: It is the recipe Lu Yu wrote down — a drink that requires a book, graded water and timed boils, already a world away from chewed Yunnan leaves.

stops.note: In 1074 the Song court established the Chamasi (Tea and Horse Office) to trade Sichuan and Yunnan tea for Tibetan warhorses; annual exchange exceeded 20,000 horses. The format was forced by the route: pressed bricks of tough leaves, twigs and stems.
stops.use: Brick tea churned with yak butter and salt into po cha — a hot, salty, fatty broth delivering calories, electrolytes and vitamins in a meat-and-barley diet. Tibet grows no tea and never did; the drink exists only because of the road. Bricks became currency by the 11th century.

highlightDish.name: Po cha (Tibetan butter tea)
highlightDish.blurb: Brick-tea broth churned with yak butter and salt; working households drink 30–60 cups a day.
highlightDish.why: The most complete transformation in the journey — the same species, the opposite of Tang refinement; every “wrong” element (salty, buttery, bitter grades) is a precise answer to altitude.

stops.note: The Song court abandoned boiling for whisking. The tribute system produced 41 varieties of Jianzhou tea; the best cakes cost more than gold.
stops.use: Powdered tea as competitive art — dou cha (“tea battles”) judged teas by the froth in black Jian-ware bowls; Chan monasteries adopted it to stay alert through meditation, the seed of chanoyu.

highlightDish.name: Song whisked bowl (dian cha)
highlightDish.blurb: Powdered Jianzhou tea frothed in a black tenmoku bowl, judged on foam.
highlightDish.why: An entire ceramics industry existed to serve whisked tea; when the Ming abandoned whisking, the blackware industry collapsed with it.

stops.note: The Zen monk Eisai returned from Song China in 1191 with seeds and the Song powdered-tea method; Sen no Rikyu (1522–1591) later codified chanoyu around wabi. Japan preserved the Song whisked style that China itself abandoned after 1391.
stops.use: Powdered matcha whisked Song-style, first as a monastic meditation aid (caffeine plus L-theanine: alert calm), then samurai tea-battle gambling, then a spiritual discipline and national art (chado). The technique is Chinese; the ritualisation Japanese.

highlightDish.name: Koicha (thick tea) in chanoyu
highlightDish.blurb: Powdered matcha whisked dense in a shared bowl, Rikyu's wabi style.
highlightDish.why: The Song whisked bowl still alive — Japan's transformation was preservation-through-refinement: the same dian cha technique, turned from imperial competition into a religion of quiet.

stops.note: The Dutch VOC made the first regular tea shipments to Europe around 1610; the conventional turning point is Catherine of Braganza's 1662 marriage to Charles II, carrying the Portuguese court habit to England.
stops.use: Expensive luxury drunk from porcelain, at first as medicine, then fashion. English drinkers added milk and sugar early — and the sugar locked tea to the Caribbean slave economy. Pitt cut the duty from 119% to 12.5% in 1784, and tea fell within working-class reach.

highlightDish.name: Tea with milk
highlightDish.blurb: Strong black tea whitened with milk and sweetened — the ancestor of builder's tea.
highlightDish.why: The specifically English transformation: no Chinese or Japanese drinker put milk in tea. Britain did not adopt tea; it domesticated it.

stops.note: The near-bankrupt East India Company got the Tea Act (May 1773): it could sell directly to the colonies, undercutting even smuggled Dutch tea. On December 16, 1773, Sons of Liberty destroyed 342 chests in Boston Harbor.
stops.use: The tea was Bohea black, the everyday British drink. The protest was not against price — the Act made tea cheaper — but against the Company monopoly and the retained Townshend duty. Parliament answered with the Intolerable Acts.

highlightDish.name: The undrunk Bohea
highlightDish.blurb: The 342 chests dumped into the harbor, never brewed.
highlightDish.why: Every other stop's highlight is a way of drinking; Boston's is a way of not drinking — proof that tea had become so embedded in imperial finance that refusing it was the sharpest political statement available.

stops.note: The indigenous Assam plant was confirmed as true tea in the 1830s; the first Company batch reached London in 1838. Then Robert Fortune, in disguise (1848–51), smuggled ~20,000 plants, ~17,000 seeds and eight Chinese craftsmen to Assam and Darjeeling in Wardian cases.
stops.use: Plantation monoculture worked by indentured labourers, making strong, malty assamica black tea built for milk — the exact leaf the English milk cup needed. By 1900 only about 10% of Britain's tea came from China.

highlightDish.name: Malty Assam black tea with milk
highlightDish.blurb: The strong plantation breakfast cup.
highlightDish.why: The product the whole operation was built for — once processing made an assamica leaf that could take milk and sugar, that cup displaced China in the British market.

stops.note: James Taylor planted 19 acres of tea on a coffee estate in 1867; when coffee rust wiped out Ceylon's coffee in 1869, ruined planters pivoted to tea. Lipton then bought failed estates cheaply, mechanised production and sold direct in branded tins.
stops.use: High-elevation plantation black tea, machine-rolled and fired at scale — Lipton's branding turned tea from a taxed luxury into a mass commodity, the template for modern packaged tea.

highlightDish.name: Lipton-style branded Ceylon cup
highlightDish.blurb: Machine-made high-grown tea from a printed tin, taken with milk and sugar.
highlightDish.why: The tin is the transformation: Taylor proved Ceylon could grow tea; Lipton proved a brand could sell it to millions, completing the journey from imperial tribute to supermarket shelf.

journeys.name: Cacao / Chocolate
journeys.tagline: From an Amazonian pulp beer to the world's smoothest confection
journeys.framing: One tree, Theobroma cacao, that moved from an Upper Amazon pulp drink to a Maya ritual foam, an Aztec currency-drink, a sweetened Spanish court luxury, an industrial powder, an English bar, a Swiss texture, and a West African smallholder crop, with every stop changing what chocolate actually is.

sources.label: Zarrillo et al. 2018, cacao domestication in the Upper Amazon (Nature Ecology and Evolution)
Wikipedia, History of chocolate
Wikipedia, Coenraad Johannes van Houten
Wikipedia, Peter's Chocolate

stops.note: The homeland: three independent evidence lines (starch grains, theobromine residues, ancient cacao DNA) date cacao use here to c. 5,450–5,300 years ago — predating any Mesoamerican evidence by about 1.5 millennia. Genetic diversity points to the upper Amazon as the centre of origin.
stops.use: Form unknown in detail, but the sweet white pulp around the beans — not the bitter beans — is the most likely first attraction: ethnography records cacao used for fermented pulp beer (cacao chicha), not bean processing. Ritual contexts from the start.

highlightDish.name: Fermented cacao-pulp drink (cacao chicha)
highlightDish.blurb: The sweet white mucilage of the pod, fermented into a low-alcohol brew.
highlightDish.why: The most honest reconstruction of the first cacao product — before grinding, roasting or foam existed; it kills the assumption that chocolate was always about the bean.

stops.note: Carried north from the Amazon — overland through Colombia and Panama, coastal canoe trade, or both (the path is unresolved). Mass-spectrometry found theobromine in vessels here (1900–1500 BCE) and at Olmec El Manati (1650–1500 BCE).
stops.use: Early Formative peoples processed and drank liquid cacao from serving vessels in ceremonies. The earliest drinks were likely fermented from the sweet pulp; the bitter bean-based drink developed later.

highlightDish.name: Mokaya liquid cacao from a spouted vessel
highlightDish.blurb: Ground, bean-based cacao served as a drink — no spices, no foam, no sugar.
highlightDish.why: It marks the pivot from pulp beer to the bean drink — the entire premise of everything after.

stops.note: The Maya were drinking cacao by about 600 CE, growing it in the tropical lowlands and trading it north. Glyphic vases show a lord presented with frothing cacao; beans were also money — 100 beans for a turkey, one for a tamale.
stops.use: Kakaw — roasted, ground beans beaten with water into a bitter, foam-crowned liquid, spiced with chili, vanilla, flowers or honey. Foam was the prestige marker: the liquid was poured from vessel to vessel from a height.

highlightDish.name: Maya beaten cacao with chili
highlightDish.blurb: Bitter cacao frothed by pouring between vessels, foam crowned.
highlightDish.why: Everything distinctive about the Maya transformation exists to serve the foam — and the foam is what the Spanish court would later abandon.

stops.note: The Aztecs inherited Maya cacao culture without growing it — cacao cannot grow in the arid Valley of Mexico, so the empire pulled it in as tribute, making it even more precious. Cortés entered in 1519; Bernal Díaz recorded Moctezuma being served 50 jars of foaming chocolatl. (The “50 cups a day” is questioned by scholars; the 50 jars are the source.)
stops.use: Xocolatl — finely ground, foamy, bitter, reddish drink with chili water, flowers, vanilla and wild bee honey; reserved for nobility and warriors, drunk cold from golden goblets. Beans served as currency throughout the empire.

highlightDish.name: Moctezuma's court xocolatl
highlightDish.blurb: Beaten cacao, chilled, spiced with vanilla and chili, served in a golden cup.
highlightDish.why: The last purely Mesoamerican stop and the version the Spanish actually tasted — everything Spain later changed (sugar, heat, milk) is measured against this cold, bitter, foamy baseline.

stops.note: Cortés returned to Spain with beans and brewing gear in 1528; by 1580 regular consignments shipped, and Spain began large-scale colonial cultivation. (Treat the “century of secrecy” story as anecdote, not settled history.)
stops.use: Spain sweetened the bitter brew with cane sugar and spiced it with cinnamon and vanilla — it became a fashionable, expensive drink of nobility and clergy, and the demand for the sweetened version drove the colonial plantation system.

highlightDish.name: Chocolate a la española
highlightDish.blurb: Thick drinking chocolate, sweetened with cane sugar, spiced with cinnamon and vanilla, served hot.
highlightDish.why: Sugar is the European transformation in a cup — the first chocolate made to please rather than to consecrate, and the formula Europe kept for two centuries.

stops.note: The drink leaked out of Spain with the decline of Spanish power: Italy c. 1606, France 1615, England 1657 (the first chocolate house “reputedly” opened by a Frenchman — widely repeated, thinly sourced). At 10–15 shillings a pound it stayed strictly for the rich.
stops.use: Drinking chocolate as a fashionable public luxury, served alongside coffee and tea — but still a drink only; nobody in 1657 was eating chocolate.

highlightDish.name: London chocolate-house drinking chocolate
highlightDish.blurb: Spiced, sugared drinking chocolate served by the cup in a commercial house.
highlightDish.why: The commercialisation moment — the drink stops being a royal secret and becomes a product, the precondition for everything industrial that follows.

stops.note: In 1828 a hydraulic press was patented in the Netherlands, pressing the fat (cocoa butter) out of ground beans — butter content from about 53% down to ~27%, leaving a cake for cocoa powder. Correction: the patent was Casparus van Houten Sr.'s, not his son Coenraad's (Coenraad's step was the alkaline “Dutching”).
stops.use: The press split the bean into two industrial products: defatted cocoa powder for cheaper drinking chocolate, and freed cocoa butter — without which there is no chocolate bar.

highlightDish.name: Dutch-process cocoa powder hot chocolate
highlightDish.blurb: Alkaline-treated cocoa powder stirred into hot water or milk, dark and mild.
highlightDish.why: The direct product of the press — one machine created both halves of modern chocolate, and this cup is the cheap half that democratised the drink.

stops.note: In 1847 J.S. Fry & Sons combined cocoa butter with chocolate liquor and sugar to produce eating chocolate, moulded into a bar — made possible by the press's freed cocoa butter.
stops.use: For the first time chocolate was solid food, not a drink — a paste of sugar, liquor and added cocoa butter pressed into a mould. Gritty and bitter by modern standards, but the form was new.

highlightDish.name: Fry's 1847 eating chocolate bar
highlightDish.blurb: Dark, gritty, moulded.
highlightDish.why: The first of its species — every later refinement (milk, conching, tempering) is an edit of this object.

stops.note: Two Swiss steps. Daniel Peter used Nestlé's condensed milk in a dehydrated “crumb” process to commercialise the first solid milk chocolate (1875; Britannica gives 1876). Then Rodolphe Lindt's 1879 conche: long, warm agitation that makes chocolate smooth, creamy and low in acidity.
stops.use: Milk chocolate as a solid bar and conching as the texture standard — smooth, melting, mild. Cadbury then scaled it: Dairy Milk launched 1905.

highlightDish.name: Conched Swiss milk chocolate bar
highlightDish.blurb: Milk chocolate, smooth from the conche, Gala Peter style.
highlightDish.why: The texture victory — the conche is invisible in the bar but unmistakable on the tongue; every smooth chocolate since 1879 is Lindt's idea wearing someone else's wrapper.

stops.note: Cacao went from Brazil to São Tomé and Fernando Po in 1840; Tetteh Quarshie, a Ga blacksmith, returned in 1879 with Amelonado pods and planted them at Mampong-Akuapem — and this planting spread. (Dutch missionaries planted earlier in 1815 and Basel missionaries in 1857; the bean-smuggling story is legend.)
stops.use: West African smallholder production: hand-harvested pods, heap fermentation under plantain leaves, sun-drying, then export as bulk beans. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana now control over 60% of global supply.

highlightDish.name: The modern mass-market milk chocolate bar
highlightDish.blurb: Grown in West Africa, made in Europe.
highlightDish.why: The only honest dish for this stop, because Ghana mostly exports beans rather than eating chocolate — the bar makes the divorce visible: cacao grown by a West African smallholder, shipped 5,000 km before it ever met milk.

journeys.name: Maize
journeys.tagline: Nine thousand years of one grass: tortilla technology, a forgotten lime bath, and the industrial afterlife.
journeys.framing: A wild Mexican grass domesticated into a grain that fed Mesoamerican civilisations, reached Europe within a year of Columbus's return, displaced sorghum and millet across Africa, killed over 100,000 Americans who ate it without the one processing step its inventors never forgot, and is now the world's most-produced cereal, grown mostly to feed animals.

stops.note: No arrival: the homeland. Early Holocene foragers lived among stands of Balsas teosinte and began selecting it. Piperno and Ranere's team found maize starch grains and phytoliths in the cracks of grinding stones at the Xihuatoxtla shelter, radiocarbon dated to c. 8,700 years before present — the earliest dated evidence of domesticated maize anywhere. Squash phytoliths appear in the same layers: maize and squash were domesticated and eaten together from the start.
stops.use: Grain as ground food, not yet as cobs. The evidence is starch on grinding tools, so the honest first form is porridge or gruel made from ground kernels — teosinte's tiny, hard grains slowly selected toward something worth grinding.

highlightDish.name: Stone-ground maize gruel (proto-atole)
highlightDish.blurb: Warm porridge of ground early maize, flour and water.
highlightDish.why: The evidence is ground starch, not cobs, so gruel is the only honest 'first dish.' It shows maize before it looked like maize — no golden ears, just the beginning of a 9,000-year kitchen.

stops.note: Domesticated maize carried east and uphill from the Balsas lowlands into the Oaxacan highlands, where it shows up as actual cobs — the oldest known maize macrofossils, dated to c. 4280 cal. BCE. But the cobs are unimpressive: 2–4 rows of kernels, a few centimetres long, on plants whose DNA shows the domestication syndrome was not yet fixed. Some 2,500 years after the Balsas, the plant was still barely improved.
stops.use: Eaten roasted or chewed, a minor supplementary crop among foraged and farmed foods; it did not become a dietary staple until much larger multi-rowed varieties appeared.

highlightDish.name: Roasted primitive cob
highlightDish.blurb: A finger-sized, 2-rowed ear eaten off the fire.
highlightDish.why: It is the anti-icon. Every later stop's maize is plumper and more productive; this one shows how little there was to work with, and how much selection the plant still had ahead of it.

stops.note: Maize crossed from Mexico into the Southwest via highland corridors along the Sierra Madre, introduced 'no later than 2100 cal. B.C.' on multiple AMS radiocarbon dates. A DNA study of ancient cobs found a second, later introduction along the Pacific coast lowlands about 2,000 years after the first — bigger cobs and kernels, 'a real improvement.' It reached the Eastern Woodlands around 200 BCE but only displaced the native crops around 900 CE, once day-length-adapted varieties evolved — feeding Cahokia just before its rise.
stops.use: Planted in floodwater-irrigated fields as a grain supplement to foraging and later to beans and squash — the 'three sisters' partnership that became the basis of Pueblo agriculture.

highlightDish.name: Hopi piki bread
highlightDish.blurb: Paper-thin blue-corn bread cooked on a hot stone, made with blue cornmeal mixed with culinary ash.
highlightDish.why: Piki is the living descendant of the desert Southwest's answer to maize — the ash is the Southwest's own alkaline trick, echoing nixtamalization independently, and the blue corn shows the crop fully indigenised to Pueblo culture thousands of years after it arrived.

stops.note: No new grain arrived — the transformation happened to the grain itself. Somewhere in Mesoamerica, cooks discovered nixtamalization: soaking and cooking dried maize in an alkaline bath, with the earliest equipment evidence from Guatemala's southern coast, 1200–1500 BCE. The alkaline bath freed the bound niacin so the body could absorb it, improved the protein balance, added calcium, and made the kernels grindable. The CDC notes explicitly that lime treatment prevents pellagra in Mexico and Central America — without this one step, everything that followed in Europe and the American South would have happened here instead.
stops.use: Nixtamalized kernels washed, hulled, and ground on the metate into masa — the dough for tortillas baked on the comal, tamales steamed in corn husks, and atole. With beans supplying the lysine maize lacks, the maize-bean-squash milpa became a complete diet. Maize became tribute, ritual, and the civilizational staple of the Maya and Aztec worlds.

highlightDish.name: The corn tortilla
highlightDish.blurb: Nixtamal, ground, patted, and baked on the comal.
highlightDish.why: The tortilla is nixtamalization made edible. Every tortilla is a dose of bioavailable niacin, and the tortilla-bean pairing is the complete protein that fed cities. It is the single most important food technology in the dossier, and it fits in your hand.

stops.note: Columbus brought maize back to Spain in 1493; Pedro Mártir de Anglería's letter of 13 November 1493 to Rome already describes the grain, and a 1494 letter says seeds were being sent to Rome — maize reached Italy within a year of Columbus's return, and spread around the Mediterranean within 25 years. Europeans misnamed it on sight: grano turco in Italy, 'Turkish wheat' in English. Nobody brought the lime bath.
stops.use: In northern Italy maize replaced spelt, millet, and buckwheat in pulmentum, the ancient grain porridge — becoming polenta. Venetian estate owners pushed it as the cheap food of peasants too poor for bread. Crucially, polenta was boiled cornmeal and water: no alkali, no beans on the side.

highlightDish.name: Polenta
highlightDish.blurb: Coarse cornmeal boiled and stirred in the copper paiolo.
highlightDish.why: Polenta is the evidence of the missing step. Same porridge form Rome had eaten for a millennium, same yellow grain as the tortilla's — but made without alkali, it carried a slow epidemic. The dish proves that with maize, the technique was the nutrition.

stops.note: First African introductions came around the mid-16th century — Cape Verde, the Canaries, São Tomé — carried by Portuguese sailors along the routes that also fed the slave trade; maize was known in Africa as 'wheat of Portugal.' A Dutch traveler wrote in 1668 that it had been carried 'from the West Indies' to São Tomé and distributed along the Gold Coast. By the late 17th century it had largely replaced millet and sorghum along the coast; in Malawi the saying is chimanga ndi moyo, 'maize is life.'
stops.use: West African farmers adopted it because it grew like sorghum but yielded far more. Ground into flour for stiff porridges, and — the distinctively West African transformation — fermented: Ghanaian kenkey is fermented maize dough steamed in corn husks. Fermentation was a second, independent answer to the grain's digestibility.

highlightDish.name: Ga kenkey
highlightDish.blurb: Fermented maize dough wrapped and steamed in corn husks.
highlightDish.why: Kenkey is not a copy of masa. Fermentation plus the husk wrapper is West Africa's own technology applied to the American grain — proof that each stop reinvented maize rather than inheriting it.

stops.note: The South's poor ate maize in a new way: degerminated white cornmeal, molasses, and fatback pork — cheap, filling, and niacin-poor. Pellagra, endemic in southern Europe for two centuries, was first reported in the US in 1902 and reached epidemic proportions in the South between 1906 and 1940: widely cited totals put it at over 3 million cases and more than 100,000 deaths. Joseph Goldberger of the US Public Health Service proved at the Spartanburg Pellagra Hospital (founded 1914) that diet — more milk, eggs, beans, peas, less cornmeal — prevented and cured it; the specific micronutrient was identified as niacin. WWII flour enrichment ended the American epidemic.
stops.use: Cornmeal as survival food — cornbread, grits, mush — without nixtamalization and without the bean pairing. Maize's niacin is chemically bound and its main protein is low in tryptophan, so a maize-dominant diet without alkali treatment starves the body of B3.

highlightDish.name: Southern cornbread
highlightDish.blurb: Baked white cornmeal, no lime bath, no beans beside it.
highlightDish.why: It is chemically the tortilla's twin and nutritionally its opposite. The 4 Ds (diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, death) lived in the difference between this bread and a comal tortilla — the dossier's starkest proof that technique, not the grain, was the whole story.

stops.note: No new grain — a new genetics. In 1917 Donald Jones crossed two single-cross hybrids — the double cross — producing seed abundantly enough to sell. Adoption was explosive: in Illinois, hybrid plantings went from barely 1% in 1932 to over 75% by 1936. Seed became a purchased annual input and yields doubled — the economic foundation of the modern grain system, and the template for the Green Revolution's seed-and-input package worldwide.
stops.use: Dent corn as a commodity — hybrid seed bought fresh every year, grown in monoculture with fertilizer and machinery. Maize stopped being food first: it became feed for livestock, starch for industry, and later ethanol and syrup.

highlightDish.name: Cornflakes
highlightDish.blurb: Toasted, boxed, branded flakes, invented in Battle Creek, Michigan in 1894.
highlightDish.why: Cornflakes were the first maize product designed for a factory rather than a kitchen — and their mass era is the hybrid-corn era. The flake is the emblem of the grain's industrial afterlife: the same species as the Balsas gruel, now a trademark.
