journeys.name: Black Pepper
journeys.tagline: The berry that ransomed Rome, launched caravels, and ended up beside the salt.
journeys.framing: A wild vine berry from the Malabar Coast that became Rome's status spice, a ransom demand from a Gothic warlord, a pound of annual rent in medieval England, the cargo that sent Portugal around Africa in 1498, and — after empires fought over it for 2,000 years — the thing sitting next to the salt on your table.

stops.note: No arrival: the homeland. Black pepper (Piper nigrum) is a woody climbing vine native to the humid forests of the Western Ghats; forest communities harvested the wild berries and began cultivating the vine on supports, and by c. 2000 BCE pepper was in use across India. For the next three millennia the Malabar Coast remained the world's only significant source. The vine's range fixed the map of the world spice trade for 4,000 years — Roman fleets, Venetian fortunes, Portuguese cannon are all consequences of this plant growing in exactly one place.
stops.use: At home, pepper was never precious. Ground berries gave heat to food and drink — a digestive in Ayurvedic practice, a warming spice in everyday cooking — in a region that grew it like a weed. Used whole and ground, in broths and buttermilk drinks, as the ordinary source of pungency.

highlightDish.name: Milagu rasam
highlightDish.blurb: The thin, tamarind-pepper broth of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, sharpened with cracked black peppercorns and cumin.
highlightDish.why: Rasam is pepper before it became treasure — the everyday form, a soup whose whole point is pepper's clean heat. It proves the spice was ordinary food at origin for thousands of years before any European tasted it.

stops.note: Carried west along the trade routes linking the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and overland to the Nile — the earliest evidence that Malabar pepper had left India. One much-repeated account holds that the embalmers of the pharaoh Ramesses II (d. c. 1213 BCE) packed his nostrils with peppercorns during mummification. Sourcing caveat: this story is widely repeated but could only be traced through popular retellings — treat as reported, not established. The trade link (pepper reaching Egypt by ~1200 BCE) has enough support to stand with caution.
stops.use: Not as food — there is no evidence Egyptians cooked with pepper. It went to the dead: a preservative and ritual good for the afterlife, valued for the same properties (drying, pungency, incorruptibility) that would later make it a medicine and a status good in Rome. Its presence in a pharaoh's tomb means that by 1200 BCE pepper was already worth moving 5,000 kilometres.

highlightDish.name: No dish — and that is the argument
highlightDish.blurb: Egyptians did not cook with pepper; the berry went to the dead, not the kitchen.
highlightDish.why: The absence is the argument. Pepper's first foreign use was as funerary wealth, which fixes how it was valued before it ever touched food: as incorruptible treasure, not as dinner.

stops.note: No arrival either — the Romans came to it. Greek and Roman merchants learned to ride the monsoon winds directly across the Arabian Sea to the Chera port of Muziris (modern Pattanam, Kerala, where 2007 excavations found Roman coins, amphorae, and a wharf), described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as the great pepper market. Roman ships arrived with gold coin and left with pepper by the shipload. The direct monsoon route cut out the middlemen and let Roman demand pour gold straight into Malabar — the first time a European empire reorganised its trade around an Indian crop.
stops.use: Rome bought pepper as a luxury import and used it with conspicuous extravagance. De re coquinaria (attributed to Apicius) includes black pepper in 81% of its nearly 500 recipes — including desserts, an extravagance that signals status rather than seasoning. Pliny the Elder grumbled in Natural History (AD 77) that pepper 'has nothing to recommend it in either fruit or berry,' and complained about the vast sums Rome spent on Indian goods — which only proves how fashionable it was.

highlightDish.name: Chuttulli meen
highlightDish.blurb: Malabar grilled fish rubbed with cracked black pepper.
highlightDish.why: While Rome paid gold for the berry, the coast that grew it ate it on the day's catch. Same spice, two economies: treasure abroad, Tuesday's dinner at home.

stops.note: By sea up the Red Sea and overland through Alexandria, then by the direct monsoon route — pepper arrived in Rome in quantities large enough to be ordinary in rich kitchens and extraordinary everywhere else. When the Visigoth king Alaric besieged Rome, his ransom demand (reported by the historian Zosimus) included 3,000 pounds of pepper — listed alongside 5,000 pounds of gold, 30,000 of silver, 4,000 silk tunics, and 3,000 scarlet hides. Correction on the record: the ransom belongs to Alaric's first siege of December 408, not the famous sack of 410 — the siege was lifted after payment.
stops.use: Pepper did three jobs in Rome: flavour (in nearly everything Apicius wrote down, savoury and sweet), medicine (Dioscorides, Celsus, and Galen list uses from digestion to tooth extraction), and stored value. A besieging army wanted pepper like it wanted gold.

highlightDish.name: Apician dulcia
highlightDish.blurb: Spiced sweet cakes and egg dishes with pepper; Roman writers describe cooks stirring as much as two tablespoons of pepper into a dish of four eggs.
highlightDish.why: Pepper in dessert is the tell. Nobody needs pepper in cake; putting it there says 'I can afford to burn money on flavour.' The dish is status, plated.

stops.note: With Rome gone, Arab merchants took over the westward trade: Malabar pepper sailed to Red Sea and Persian Gulf ports, crossed to Alexandria, and was bought there by Venetian (and Genoese) merchants who held a near-monopoly on redistribution into Europe. Each handoff multiplied the price. The Arab-Venetian markup chain is also what made the direct sea route worth dying for: every middleman's cut was an argument for sailing around Africa.
stops.use: In medieval Europe pepper was seasoning, medicine, and — crucially — money. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that medieval 'peppercorn rents' were not the nominal token of modern law: they were typically an obligation to pay a pound of pepper on rent days, 'a substantial impost even as late as the 18th century.' Rent, dowry, bribe, and tax could all be paid in it.

highlightDish.name: Cameline sauce
highlightDish.blurb: The most-cited sauce of medieval France (some fifty 14th–15th-century recipes): cinnamon 'in great abundance,' ginger, cloves, grains of paradise, and pepper, ground with bread and sharpened with vinegar or wine, served with roast meats.
highlightDish.why: Cameline shows pepper's demotion beginning — no longer the solo star as in Rome, now one voice in a luxury chorus. The spice that once ransomed a city is now a line item in a sauce recipe.

stops.note: On 20 May 1498 Vasco da Gama's fleet reached Kappadu near Calicut after rounding Africa — asked what brought them, the Portuguese answered 'in search of Christians and spices.' The pepper trade, not the fine spices of the Moluccas, was the voyage's economic target. What followed was conquest as trade policy: Cabral's 1500 factory destroyed, da Gama's 1502 bombardment of the port, a factory at Cochin in 1503, Goa seized in 1510. Portugal made the Indian pepper trade a royal monopoly, enforced by the cartaz (pass) system — trade at cannon-point. The 'age of exploration' was, on its Portuguese leg, a pepper war.
stops.use: Portugal's achievement was logistical, not culinary: they moved the pepper trade from the Alexandria-Venice chain to the Cape route and sold it cheaper in Europe than Venice could, breaking the old monopoly. At the source, nothing changed about how pepper was eaten — it stayed the everyday heat of Malabar cooking.

highlightDish.name: Kozhi milagu varuval
highlightDish.blurb: Kerala chicken fried with crushed black peppercorns.
highlightDish.why: Five centuries of empires fought over this berry, and at home it never stopped being what it was — the heat itself, crushed fresh over chicken. The dish is the anti-monopoly: pepper as food, not as finance.

stops.note: In 1663 the Dutch East India Company (VOC) helped the Raja of Cochin expel the Portuguese and took the Malabar pepper monopoly for itself. The VOC then did what monopolists do: it destroyed pepper cargoes to keep prices high. It didn't work. By mid-century Europe was awash in pepper: prices fell about 40% from the levels Portugal and the VOC had maintained, and Dutch and English East India Company imports peaked around 7 million kilograms in 1670, then fell to about 3.5 million by 1688. The companies pivoted to the new trades — tea, coffee, cotton, opium.
stops.use: Pepper lost its status as an exotic luxury and became a mundane commodity — the end of its 2,000-year run as treasure. Seventeenth-century cookbooks (La Varenne, 1651) show simpler, less-spiced cooking. The spice that ransomed Rome and launched caravels was now cheap enough to bake into children's biscuits.

highlightDish.name: Speculaas
highlightDish.blurb: The traditional Dutch spiced biscuit, born in the 17th-century trading boom: cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, ginger, cardamom, and black pepper in the spice mix, pressed in wooden molds.
highlightDish.why: Speculaas is the monopoly era fossilised in dough. The berries that once came home in armed carracks, worth a pound of silver per pound, ended up as one note in a holiday cookie — pepper's whole arc from treasure to pantry, in a single bite.

stops.note: The vine left home for good. After the Portuguese carried Malabar vines to Southeast Asia in the 16th century, pepper farming slowly spread; in the late 20th century Vietnam industrialised it. In 1980 Vietnam harvested just 556 tonnes while India harvested more than fifty times as much; by the early 2000s Vietnam had overtaken India, and on 2022 FAO figures it grew 272,235 tonnes — more than a third of world production, over twice second-place Brazil, with India down to 64,205 t. The 4,000-year Malabar monopoly ended not by conquest but by agronomy.
stops.use: Pepper as pure plantation commodity: intensive monoculture, high yields (Vietnamese farms produce roughly five times per hectare what Indian smallholdings do), traded on world markets with India itself now a major buyer. The berry's birthplace is a minor producer of its own native crop.

highlightDish.name: Cacio e pepe
highlightDish.blurb: Rome's three-ingredient pasta: tonnarelli, Pecorino Romano, and black pepper, no more.
highlightDish.why: After 4,000 years, pepper finally got a dish named for it. Not a ransom, not a rent, not a monopoly — just the berry, celebrated for itself. The status spice came home to being food.

journeys.name: Cinnamon
journeys.tagline: An island bark lied about for two millennia: funeral pyres, monopolies, and the Swedish coffee break.
journeys.framing: A tree bark from one island that became the ancient world's most lied-about luxury — guarded by invented monsters in the stories, by empires in reality — and then collapsed from a year's wages per pound to a supermarket staple, ending up as the defining flavor of Mexican chocolate and the Swedish work break.

stops.note: No arrival — this is the tree's home. Wild Cinnamomum verum grew in the island's forests; the peeling craft is a Sri Lankan invention, likely centuries old by the time Europeans arrived. The quill is the technology: bark peeled in the rainy season, scraped, curled into nested tubes that dry into the familiar stick. The island developed the world's only skilled cinnamon-peeling labor force — a hereditary caste (the Salagama/Kurundukara) whose expertise would become, under Europeans, a resource to be captured rather than a craft to be honored. Five to seven years to master the peel.
stops.use: On the island itself the bark went into medicine first — research by Dr Dilhani Dissanayake finds cinnamon was used as a traditional Ayurvedic medicine before it became a cooking spice — and later into the island's curries as a background warmth. Never the star, the way it would become abroad.

highlightDish.name: Sri Lankan chicken curry with cinnamon bark
highlightDish.blurb: A true cinnamon quill simmered into coconut-milk curry alongside cardamom and cloves.
highlightDish.why: It shows the bark at home, where it was always a supporting spice. Every later stop treats cinnamon as the precious cargo; here it is just one warmth among many in the island's own kitchen — proof that the luxury story was invented at the far end of the trade route, not at its source.

stops.note: Dried bark arriving from the east via Red Sea and Arabian middlemen — 'imported to Egypt as early as 2000 BC' is the widely repeated date, though which bark (true cinnamon or cassia) is debated, and direct archaeobotanical evidence is thin. The dossier keeps the stop with 'c.' and a debate note instead of asserting it. The bark's first transformation was into wealth: once Egyptians wanted it for the afterlife, demand no longer depended on taste — it depended on belief.
stops.use: Not food — ritual. Egypt used aromatic barks in embalming and temple rites: the strong scent masked the smell of the dead, and the bark's chemistry helped preserve tissue. It was also perfume — a sacred substance for the dead and the gods, a medicine and a status marker.

highlightDish.name: Kyphi
highlightDish.blurb: The sacred temple incense (myrrh, honey, wine, and aromatic barks including cinnamon/cassia) burned in evening rites.
highlightDish.why: It is not food, and that is the point. Kyphi proves that for two thousand years cinnamon's first and most important job in the West was religious — cooked never, burned always.

stops.note: Bark carried by Arabian caravans into the Levant's ports and overland routes. The Hebrew Bible's texts, composed across the Iron Age, name it repeatedly: Exodus 30:23 commands Moses to take 'sweet cinnamon' (qinnamon) and cassia for the holy anointing oil; Proverbs 7:17 perfumes the bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon; the Song of Songs 4:14 lists cinnamon among the garden's chief spices; Revelation 18:13 would later list it among Babylon's mourned luxuries.
stops.use: Still not food — sacred perfume and seduction. In the Bible the bark sits beside gold and precious stones as a measure of value. The bark entered the moral imagination of the West as the smell of holiness and of forbidden pleasure at once — the association that would make medieval Christians treat it as medicine and aristocrats as display.

highlightDish.name: The holy anointing oil
highlightDish.blurb: Olive oil blended with myrrh, sweet cinnamon, sweet calamus, and cassia (Exodus 30:23).
highlightDish.why: Why this 'dish': it is a recipe, measured and mixed, just never eaten. It proves the bark's status before it ever touched food: an ingredient of consecration, where the cinnamon in the blend is the expensive half of the formula.

stops.note: No arrival — the homeland of Cinnamomum cassia (Chinese cinnamon), a different tree, a thicker, harder, more pungent bark, native to southern China and mainland Southeast Asia. And for most of history, when a Western text said 'cinnamon,' this is often what actually arrived: the two barks were confused in trade for millennia, and 'cinnamon' and 'cassia' were sold as separate grades of the same luxury in Rome.
stops.use: Cassia went into Chinese medicine and cooking — the bark that braises with star anise and soy, that grinds into five-spice, that flavors red-braised meats. Where true cinnamon is sweet and citrusy, cassia is hot and woody, with far more coumarin. It was the cheaper substitute that traveled better, and it won the modern supermarket: roughly 95% of what is sold as 'cinnamon' in the US today is cassia.

highlightDish.name: Hong shao rou
highlightDish.blurb: Red-braised pork belly with cassia bark, star anise, and soy.
highlightDish.why: It is the honest home of the bark that pretended to be cinnamon for three thousand years. Cassia here is not a substitute; it is the intended flavor — woody, assertive, the backbone of the braise — showing what the 'other' bark is when it is not being mislabeled.

stops.note: Bark shipped from Arabia and the Red Sea trade, marked up at every handoff, bought by Romans who had no idea where it grew. Pliny the Elder complained that Indian and Arabian imports sold in Rome at a hundred times their cost, and that the cinnamon trade was riddled with adulteration — even he could not say exactly where the tree grew. At Poppaea Sabina's funeral in 65 CE, Nero reportedly burned more cinnamon and cassia than the producing countries yielded in a year (Pliny, Natural History 12.41: framed as Pliny's report, 'experts claim...', not a measured fact).
stops.use: Funeral pyres, perfume oils, and spiced wine. Cinnamon unguent (perfume oil) sold for 35 to 300 denarii a pound — note: the price of the perfume preparation, often misquoted as the raw bark. They inherited the monster stories: Herodotus (c. 450 BCE) had recorded giant birds carrying cinnamon sticks to cliff nests, tales Roman writers repeated, which served the Arab middlemen's interest.

highlightDish.name: Conditum paradoxum
highlightDish.blurb: Roman spiced wine from Apicius, wine steeped with honey, pepper, and aromatic barks including cinnamon/cassia.
highlightDish.why: It is the ancestor of every European mulled wine to come. It proves Rome had already moved cinnamon from the pyre toward the cup — the first step in the bark's two-thousand-year migration from ritual to recipe.

stops.note: Bark bought from Arab merchants at Alexandria and the Levantine ports, shipped to Venice, and redistributed across Europe at monopoly prices. Venice's near-monopoly on the eastern spice trade made cinnamon ruinously expensive — the prices that pushed Portugal to look for a sea route around Africa.
stops.use: Medicine and aristocratic cookery. In the humoral kitchen, wine was 'cold and dry,' so warm spices — cinnamon first — were added to balance it: hippocras, the spiced wine of medieval banquets. Le Viandier de Taillevent (c. 1300) gives a hippocras powder that begins 'four ounces of very fine cinnamon, two ounces of fine cassia flowers...' — cinnamon as the main spice, not a garnish. Cooks put it in sauces, meat dishes, and sweets; doctors prescribed it.

highlightDish.name: Hippocras
highlightDish.blurb: Red or white wine steeped with ground cinnamon (the dominant spice), ginger, cloves, and sugar, filtered clear.
highlightDish.why: It is the medieval European use of cinnamon in its purest form — cinnamon as medicine, status, and pleasure in a single cup, and the recipe survives verbatim from 1300. Every later European cinnamon dessert descends from this spiced-wine logic.

stops.note: In 1505 Dom Lourenço de Almeida's squadron, driven by storm, put into Galle; the king of Kotte offered cinnamon and elephants and, in the treaty that followed, agreed to gift Portugal a large annual quantity of cinnamon (one account puts it at about 200,000 pounds a year — treat as the treaty's reported scale, not a measured export statistic). In 1517–18 the Portuguese built their fort at Colombo and turned the gift into a monopoly: by 1614 the cinnamon trade was a Portuguese royal monopoly. The lie died — for the first time, Europeans stood in the cinnamon forests and saw that there were no giant birds, just trees, peelers, and a king's tax system.
stops.use: Tribute, not trade. The Portuguese took over the island's existing system — Salagama peelers delivering quills as tax to the king — and scaled it with forced labor. In Portugal the bark went into the sweet kitchen, notably the custard desserts that carry cinnamon to this day.

highlightDish.name: Leite-creme
highlightDish.blurb: The Portuguese baked custard finished with a dusting of ground cinnamon (the ancestor of crème brûlée).
highlightDish.why: It is the first European dessert where cinnamon is not medicine or ritual but pure pleasure — the bark's arrival in the sweet kitchen, made possible only because Portuguese ships now sailed straight to the source instead of buying from Venice at tenth hand.

stops.note: The VOC, allied with inland Kandy against the Portuguese, took Galle in 1640 and stormed Colombo in 1658, expelling the Portuguese by 1659. The cinnamon monopoly passed to the Dutch East India Company, which ran it as a military operation: registered trees, forced peeler labor under brutal discipline (floggings, brandings, mutilations documented in contemporary research), and the destruction of cinnamon trees outside VOC control to keep supply scarce and prices high. When Britain seized Ceylon in 1796 and the monopoly broke, prices began their long fall.
stops.use: The quill trade at industrial scale. Cinnamon gardens were planted under VOC control; peelers worked under quotas. In Europe the bark remained a luxury through the 18th century — and the British proved the corollary of the Dutch monopoly by breaking it: once competition returned, cinnamon began its slide from imperial commodity to household spice.

highlightDish.name: Lamprais
highlightDish.blurb: The Dutch Burgher rice parcel of Sri Lanka: rice, meat curries (with cinnamon bark among the spices), and sambol, wrapped in banana leaf and baked.
highlightDish.why: It is the island's own cuisine absorbing the colonizers' table. While the VOC burned trees to keep cinnamon scarce in Europe, Sri Lankan kitchens kept cooking with it — proof the bark never stopped being a home spice even as empires fought over it as a commodity.

stops.note: Cinnamon crossed the Atlantic with the Spanish and the Pacific with the Manila galleons — the Portuguese shipped Ceylon cinnamon to the Philippines, and Spanish colonists carried it on to Mexico's Pacific ports, folding it into New Spain's kitchens and convents.
stops.use: Canela. Mexico's cinnamon is true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum) — soft, crumbly, multi-layered quills, sweet and floral — the opposite of the hard, harsh cassia that dominates US supermarket jars. It went into the drinks: chocolate caliente and champurrado (cacao, sugar, cinnamon, frothed with the molinillo), café de olla, horchata, and moles. The Spanish had taken cacao to Europe and added sugar and cinnamon to the bitter Mesoamerican drink; in Mexico, cinnamon fused with the native cacao tradition instead of replacing it.

highlightDish.name: Champurrado
highlightDish.blurb: The thick chocolate atole of masa, cacao, sugar, and canela, whisked with the molinillo.
highlightDish.why: It is the fusion made edible. Cacao is Mesoamerican; sugar and cinnamon are the colonial arrivals; the molinillo froth is the technique that binds them. One cup holds the whole route: a Sri Lankan bark, carried by Portuguese and Spanish ships, seasoning an Aztec drink.

stops.note: Cinnamon arriving cheap, by steamship and rail, as a mass commodity — the endpoint of the post-1796 price collapse. What had been worth a year's wages per pound in Rome was now affordable to Swedish home bakers. The modern kanelbulle — yeasted wheat dough, butter, sugar, cinnamon, knotted and topped with pearl sugar — was created in Sweden in the 1920s, when post-WWI prosperity put sugar, butter, and cinnamon within reach; it became a household staple in the 1950s, and Sweden gave it its own day (Kanelbullens dag, October 4, since 1999).
stops.use: The fika bun. The democratization of cinnamon is complete: the bark that emperors burned by the pound is now the smell of an ordinary Tuesday coffee break — the luxury fully dissolved into comfort, with cardamom (another once-priceless spice) riding along in the dough.

highlightDish.name: Kanelbulle
highlightDish.blurb: The knotted cinnamon-and-cardamom bun of fika.
highlightDish.why: It is the proof that the price collapse actually happened. No king, no monopoly, no medicine — just a bun, eaten by millions, whose existence depends on cinnamon being cheap. The most democratic form the bark has ever taken.
